prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing the measurement of time and frequency to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock (B049, Katori and Ye) as my single-part final position. Having read all eight statements, the case has not weakened and the objections raised against it are about classification, not about whether the result is real. The magic-wavelength lattice does something no earlier clock did: it holds a very large number of atoms in a Doppler- and recoil-free configuration without perturbing the clock transition, and that is what delivers the statistical-stability gain over single ions and the 1e-18 accuracy. The result is confirmed the way I insist on: JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE build and compare these clocks and agree at levels no other measurement can check. It has produced millimetre-scale redshift tests, bounds on variation of constants and a concrete route to redefining the second. The credited names are the cleanest on the table, with Katori carrying the concept and first realisation and Ye carrying the platform to record performance. A citation written around the magic-wavelength lattice, as all four supporters word it, leaves the comb and single-ion lineage honoured in 2005 and 2012 untouched. I have not changed my configuration since round 1; what has changed is my confidence in the answer to the chair's novelty question, which I explain in my responses.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains classification. Danielsson, Eriksson and Olsson ask whether the clock is a new door or a much better version of a door already opened, and a prize for a measurement that has not yet shown a departure from known physics will be read by some as a prize for precision. The priority record is not something I can settle from my own expertise: I recall that Katori proposed the magic-wavelength scheme in 2003 and that strontium lattice clocks followed quickly in Tokyo and at JILA, while Lemonde's group proposed and worked on lattice clocks in the same period and Hollberg and Gill worked on neutral-atom and single-ion clocks, but I am relying on memory and the atomic-physics members should check it. If the record shows an independent and simultaneous demonstration, a two-name prize may need a different citation or a third name. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so the practical payoff is still prospective. Finally, I came to this position from sixth place in my own opening ballot by deferring to colleagues in atomic physics, and I cannot independently audit Ye's contribution beyond what Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth have said.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the clock first but notes that Ye's comb and laser-stabilisation work lies partly in territory honoured in 2005, and asks that the record on who first demonstrated the lattice clock be checked.
responses.response: I accept both points and they shape my citation. Ye's stabilised-laser and comb work is not what I am crediting him for; the citation credits the realisation of the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its performance at 1e-18, so the 2005 prize is not being repeated. On who was first, I think the answer is that Katori proposed the magic wavelength and made the first strontium lattice clock, with Ye's group following and then taking accuracy and stability much further. That is memory, not a checked record, and I would ask you to confirm it from the primary papers before the vote. If it holds, the two-name attribution stands, and if the record shows Lemonde had an equal claim I would want that stated openly instead of ignored.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the clock only as an alternative because the 2005 and 2012 prizes cover the conceptual ground and the clocks have not yet shown a result from nature that changes how we think; he would rank it higher after a redefinition of the second or an anomalous result.
responses.response: I understand why you drew the line there, and I moved off IceCube partly because of your own caveat about one name for a collaboration. But I disagree that no result from nature has come out. The clocks measure the gravitational redshift over millimetres, which is a direct test of general relativity at a scale nobody could reach before, and they set the tightest laboratory limits on drifts of constants. Absence of an anomaly is still a measurement. I also do not think the prize should wait for a redefinition; the physics is confirmed by independent laboratories whatever BIPM decides. I do concede that this is a prize for an instrument, and I think we should say so plainly in the citation instead of dressing it as a discovery of a new phenomenon.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B009 because the correlated insulator and superconducting dome at the predicted angle is a new state of matter and the clock is, in his view, an extraordinary refinement of a known measurement principle rather than a surprise.
responses.response: I agree that B009 is the more surprising result and that it is my first alternative. Where I differ is on how to weigh the evidence of a young field against the evidence of an old one. Both of us accept that the open pairing mechanism is not a reason to doubt the discovery, but the committee also has to defend maturity, and the clock's results have been reproduced independently for years with attribution that fits in two names. The twisted-bilayer case still has the Cao, Fatemi and Dean-group question that you, Olsson and Danielsson each concede is open. I would reconsider if the condensed-matter members tell me that question has a clean answer within three names. Your point that the clock is a refinement is fair, but a refinement by a factor of a hundred that changes what can be measured is the kind of instrument advance this committee has honoured before.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B009 first and the clock second, wants the historical record checked on the earlier flat-band theory and the experimental co-first authors, and answers Eriksson that all three of Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero are needed.
responses.response: I agree on the Bistritzer-MacDonald pair and your reasoning that splitting a single paper would be arbitrary. The harder issue is the experimental side: if Cao, who did the hands-on 2018 work, has a stronger claim than Bistritzer, then the three-name cap forces a choice that I find hard to defend, and I am not the right person to make it. That is the reason I cannot rank B009 above the clock today. It is also why I note that your own second choice is the clock: both the condensed-matter first-place voters and the atomic-physics first-place voters put it in their top two, which makes it the one configuration where nobody has to accept something they judge unfinished. I am not counting support to settle the science, but I am saying the attribution risk is smaller for B049.

responses.point: Johansson argues that the lattice clock is a distinct step from the Wineland ion clock because many atoms at once give the stability gain, and that the SI redefinition need not come first.
responses.response: That is the argument I need for the chair's novelty question and I find it convincing: the many-atom interrogation at a magic wavelength is not available to a single ion, so the stability advantage is a new capability and not a better ion clock. I do not want to overstate it, because I have not checked the numbers myself. I also note your disclosure on B040 and agree it should be recorded, but it has no bearing on B049. Your point that I should keep the citation on the lattice and not on metrology in general is already in my wording.

uncertainties: Whether the record supports Katori as first to propose and demonstrate the lattice clock, and whether Lemonde, Hollberg or Gill have a claim strong enough to change a two-name prize; I am relying on memory and on the atomic-physics members.
Whether the committee will accept a prize for a precision instrument, with no departure from known physics yet observed, as a discovery of the kind the will of Nobel describes.

Whether twisted bilayer graphene could be credited defensibly within three names given Cao, Fatemi, Dean and earlier flat-band theory; I defer to the condensed-matter members and would reconsider if they find a clean answer.
Whether my move from sixth place to first on the strength of colleagues' expertise has made me over-weight their agreement.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: no personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or any other credited person for B049 or B009. I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, which are adjacent to B010 and B047, and I opened by ranking B010 first; neither is in my final configuration. I note Johansson's recusal on B040 and Kroll's year in the Hall laboratory at JILA, and I do not think the latter disqualifies him, but the committee should record it.
